notes:
I covered most verses with traditional commentary. My searches did not reach any Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran or Methodist pages, the NET Bible or Bible Odyssey notes, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching, so those are left out. I didn't find real disagreements between Protestant traditions either. What did turn up is several places where individual commentators disagree; I've flagged those below. Also note: the "Utley," "Bush," "Grant," "Campbell" and "Carr" comments are quoted secondhand on the Precept Austin page, and Enduring Word (David Guzik) is a Calvary Chapel source.

**Overview**
- The Gospel Coalition commentary sees the book's author covering Jericho in chapters 2–6 and Ai in 7:1–8:29. He then closes these materials with an account of Israel's covenant renewal in 8:30–35. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/joshua/)
- Ellicott says Jericho and Ai are the only two city captures told in detail, as samples of the whole conquest. At Jericho God's hand is most visible; at Ai Israel's own effort is. The whole work is thus presented to us in a twofold aspect, as the work of Israel and the work of God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-8.html)

**v. 1**
- "Do not be afraid" came after their hearts had "melted" in 7:5. Now that the sin was dealt with, God spoke again. He put the promise in the past tense ("I have delivered"), as He had at Jericho, meaning obedience was all that was needed. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-8-commentary)
- Enduring Word: losing the first battle showed God had not been with Israel. Sin practiced and unconfessed made them weak, and deservedly afraid and dismayed. With sin dealt with, they could trust in God's restoration and put away fear and dismay. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-8/)
- Ellicott: "Ai" means "the heap" (of ruins). Verse 28 calls it "a heap forever" (Hebrew *Tel-olam*), so its first and last names match. He thought this fixed the site at et-Tel. "His land" means Ai was the chief town of a territory. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-8.html)
- **Why "the whole army"?** Commentators give different reasons:
  - Bible.org: the main cause of the first defeat was Achan's sin. A secondary cause was underestimating the enemy, overestimating themselves, and presuming on the Lord. (https://bible.org/seriespage/victory-ai-joshua-81-35)
  - The Pulpit Commentary, following Calvin, says 3,000 men were not too few. It was to reassure the people, whose hearts had "melted and become as water." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/8-1.htm)
  - Gill takes it as all men over twenty (about 500,000). Bush and Clarke think it meant the 30,000 picked men. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/8-1.htm; Bush: https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-8-commentary; Clarke: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-8/)

**v. 2**
- Israel could keep the plunder this time. Matthew Henry notes that Achan grabbed forbidden spoil and lost everything, while those who obeyed were soon rewarded with Ai's spoil. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-8-commentary)
- Enduring Word: had Achan obeyed at Jericho, he could have had spoil from Ai. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-8/)
- Ellicott: the spoil meant goods, not people. Jericho was the exception because its goods were "devoted" to God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-8.html)
- **Was the ambush deceit?** Bush (on Precept Austin) says This stratagem is to be justified on the ground that God commanded it, and it is obvious that if it was right for them to overpower their enemies, it was equally right to out-wit them. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-8-commentary) Ligonier (Reformed) plainly calls the capture an elaborate deceit done at God's instruction. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/israelites-conquer-ai)

**vv. 3–9, 12 (the 30,000 and the 5,000)**
- Commentators disagree on whether there was one ambush or two. Stephen Grant describes two views:
  - One force only, the numbers being a copying error. David Howard calls this a drastic step with no manuscript support.
  - Two separate forces. A. W. Pink argues the second one cut Bethel off from Ai.
  - The Bible Knowledge Commentary sees three groups: 30,000 in ambush, the main army, and 5,000 blocking Bethel.
  
  (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-8-commentary)
- Ellicott studied the ground on the Ordnance map. He leans toward two bodies of men in two different ravines: a nearer one to burn Ai, and a larger one to block Bethel. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-8.html)
- Ligonier simply describes 5,000 hiding to the west and 25,000 to the north. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/israelites-conquer-ai)

**v. 5**
- "As they did the first time": now it was Ai's confidence from its earlier win that led it into defeat. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-8-commentary)

**v. 7**
- Israel had its part to play, but in the end God's power secured Ai. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-8-commentary)

**v. 8**
- Bush thinks "set it on fire" may mean only a signal fire, since verse 28 shows the full burning came later. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-8-commentary)
- The Gospel Coalition: Joshua reminded them to act on the Lord's word, which they had failed to do in the first battle. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/joshua/)

**v. 9**
- Grant: by spending the night with the people, Joshua showed he was not a distant leader. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-8-commentary)
- Guzik applies it to Christians: If we will regain victory, we must live with and follow Jesus, who is our Joshua. (https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Jos/Jos_8.cfm)

**v. 10**
- Enduring Word quotes Trapp: Joshua was "much noted for his early rising." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-8/)
- Ellicott: "numbered" is better translated "mustered." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-8.html)

**vv. 11, 13**
- Ellicott: the main army probably camped north of a ravine (Wady Maheesin). The "valley" in verse 13 is a wider part, chosen to draw the pursuit toward Gilgal. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-8.html)
- Grant links Joshua's night in the valley to his night near Jericho (5:13). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-8-commentary)

**v. 14**
- Guzik: Ai repeated its old tactic. Generally, Satan will stick with a strategy against us until it doesn't work anymore. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/joshua/joshua-8.cfm)

**vv. 15–16**
- God gave a completely different plan this time; the pretended defeat led to real victory. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-8/)

**v. 17**
- The mention of Bethel shows its soldiers had joined Ai's. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62600/)
- Ellicott notes it is odd that Bethel itself is not said to have been captured here. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-8.html)

**vv. 18, 26 (the raised lance)**
- Ellicott compares it to Moses holding up the rod against Amalek. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-8.html)
- Enduring Word quotes Howard: the lance was more than a starting signal; it was also a symbol of God's presence and help in the battle. In Exodus 17 Joshua was the one helped by Moses' raised arms; now he plays Moses' part. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-8/)
- Precept Austin thinks a signal had probably been agreed in advance. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-8-commentary)
- A Bible Hub study page sees the javelin as a picture of Christ's cross. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/joshua/8.htm)

**vv. 19–22**
- When the men of Ai saw the smoke, they knew they had been fooled and were beaten. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-8-commentary)
- Enduring Word quotes Morgan: the story shows the value of the best in human reason in God's work. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-8/)

**v. 23**
- The Gospel Coalition: the king was the only one left alive after the attack. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/joshua/)

**vv. 24–25**
- Clarke estimates that fewer than half of the 12,000 people were fighting men. (https://studylight.org/commentary/joshua/8-1.html)
- Matthew Henry says God had passed sentence on them for their wickedness; Israel only carried out His justice. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/8-28.html)
- Enduring Word calls this God's judgment on the Canaanites, given through Israel. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-8/)

**v. 27**
- Ellicott: Ai's spoil went to Israel, while Jericho's had been claimed for God alone. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-8.html)

**v. 28**
- Ellicott ties "heap forever" to the modern name et-Tel. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-8.html)
- The Bible Hub commentary takes "to this day" as eyewitness detail and the ruins as a reminder of what unrepented sin leads to. (https://biblehub.com/joshua/8-28.htm)

**v. 29**
- Ligonier lists three lessons:
  1. It showed God's curse was on the Canaanites.
  2. It warned other Canaanites.
  3. It reminded Israel that resisting God brings death; Achan died too.
  
  (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/israelites-conquer-ai)
- Ellicott points to Deuteronomy 21:22–23 and to Christ who fulfilled the curse of God in His own person. He says burial under stones was another form of the curse. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-8.html)
- Clarke: the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) says a "double tree," possibly a fork or cross shape. He thinks the king was probably killed before being hung. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/lat/cvl/joshua/8-29.html)

**v. 30 (when did it happen?)**
- Ellicott: Josephus dates it later, and the Septuagint puts it in a different order. Still, he sees no reason to move it, since taking Ai opened the road to Shechem. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-8.html)
- Gill notes that Ebal is far from Ai and reports a Jewish view that the altar was built five years later. The Pulpit Commentary notes that several critics call the passage an insertion. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/8-30.htm; Pulpit: https://biblehub.com/joshua/8-30.htm)
- Keil & Delitzsch: after Ai, Israel was secure enough to obey Deuteronomy 27. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/8-30.htm)

**v. 31**
- Matthew Poole (and Benson): the altar stood on Ebal, the mountain of the curses, so that the means of grace would be found where the curses were spoken. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/8-30.htm)
- Enduring Word: uncut stones show what God made, not what people made. It also mentions that a site on Ebal has been suggested as Joshua's altar. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-8/)
- Calvin calls it the first special sacrifice offered in Canaan, to set the land apart for God. (https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom07.xi.ii.html)

**v. 32**
- Bush thinks Joshua copied only the blessings and curses, not the whole Law. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62600/)
- Keil & Delitzsch think the altar probably came before the writing on the stones. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/8-30.htm)

**v. 33**
- Bush: "facing the priests" means the priests had a full view of the people. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62600/)
- Enduring Word lists which tribes stood on each mountain, with the ark between them. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-8/)

**vv. 34–35**
- Enduring Word: foreigners were included, which shows Israel's faith was missionary in nature and open to outsiders. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-8/)
- Ellicott reports that tests have shown the whole crowd could hear the reading from this spot. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-8.html)

**Other views and popular applications**
- **Archaeology (vv. 1, 28):** Constable says et-Tell matches the geography of Joshua 8 well. However, nothing has been found there from Joshua's time; it was a large city about a thousand years earlier. Some propose Khirbet el-Maqatir instead. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-7.html)
- A Themelios article on the Gospel Coalition site says some scholars use this gap to treat the story as aetiological, meaning a story told to explain an existing ruin. The author argues this reasoning is inconsistent. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/the-origins-of-israel-in-canaan-an-examination-of-recent-theories/)
- **Ai as "the flesh":** Alan Carr reads Ai as a picture of the sinful nature and the battle as how believers "ambush" it. Guzik draws a similar lesson: show no mercy to their enemy, meaning sin. (Carr: https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-8-commentary; Guzik: https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Jos/Jos_8.cfm)
